      OCTA DATA CENTER DEVELOPMENT COMPANY LLC’S COMMENTS ON
                 ERCOT’S AUGUST 10, 2026 STATUS UPDATE


TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:


        Octa Data Center Development Company LLC (Octa) files these comments in response to

the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc.’s (ERCOT) Requests for Good Cause Exceptions

Relating to Batch Zero Deadlines and Status Update on Additional Matters Including the Long-

Term Load Forecast (ERCOT Status Update), 1 filed in the above-captioned project on August 10,

2026, and respectfully shows as follows:

                                           I.       INTRODUCTION


        Octa is a powered land developer in Texas whose project portfolio includes new data center

developments under 75 MW.


        On August 3, 2026, Governor Abbott issued a letter directing the Public Utility

Commission of Texas (Commission) and ERCOT to conduct a “verification and audit” of data

center projects.2 In response, the ERCOT Status Update temporarily paused the transitional large

 load interconnection study process, commonly referred to as Batch Zero, until the verification and

audit are complete.3 However, the Batch Zero process only applies to interconnecting Large

Loads,4 which ERCOT defines as “[o]ne or more Facilities at a single site with an aggregate peak

Demand greater than or equal to 75 MW” behind a common point of interconnection. 5 For projects

under 75 MW, the requirements of Batch Zero do not apply. Governor Abbott’s August 3 letter

nonetheless requests certain information for all interconnecting data center loads—even those

loads below 75 MW. To implement this request, the ERCOT Status Update states that ERCOT

will collect “community impact information” from “all data centers and virtual currency mining

facilities greater than 25 MW and less than 75 MW that have not yet energized.” 6 Based on the

language of Governor Abbott’s letter, Octa interprets “community impact information” as

information regarding the extent data centers are reducing impacts on neighboring property owners

and communities, including (1) noise mitigation, (2) light controls, (3) property setbacks, (4) traffic

improvements, (5) emergency response coordination, and (6) other community protection

matters.7 Octa files the following comments in response to the ERCOT Status Update to clarify

the information that data center loads under 75 MW will need to provide as part of the verification

and audit process.

                        II.     COMMENTS ON ERCOT STATUS UPDATE


        Octa appreciates Governor Abbott’s and ERCOT’s commitment to ensuring a safe and

stable electric grid for all Texans. However, because projects under 75 MW have not been involved

in the Batch Zero process, many of these projects have not submitted the detailed information that

other, larger data center projects have submitted for Batch Zero consideration. Additionally, these

smaller projects are less likely to create substantial strain on the electric grid compared to the large-

scale data center projects seeking interconnection in ERCOT, some of which are more than ten

times the size of a 75 MW project. Octa understands that it will be required to provide the

community impact information described above, but it does not believe that the additional

verification and audit information otherwise required of large loads under the ERCOT Status

Update will apply to it. To ensure compliance with the ERCOT Status Update and Governor

Abbott’s letter, Octa requests clarity from ERCOT regarding the community impact information

that Octa will need to provide as part of the verification and audit process described in the ERCOT

Status Update.


        Octa further recommends that ERCOT make a distinction between projects under 75 MW

that are being developed inside municipal boundaries and those that are being developed in

unincorporated communities. Because projects located inside municipal boundaries are required

to obtain municipal permits, plat approvals, and city water/wastewater capacity commitments in

accordance with municipal guidelines, they should not be treated with the same level of scrutiny

as projects developed in unincorporated areas with much less oversight. Projects inside municipal

limits routinely work closely with local governmental officials to minimize the project’s impact

on city resources. The additional audit process outlined in the ERCOT Status Update for these

projects is duplicative of this existing local review. Community impact is most effectively assessed

                                                   3
 by the local officials accountable to the affected community. ERCOT should continue to evaluate

electric load and grid impacts through its interconnection processes, but community impact

assessments—especially for projects inside municipal boundaries—should be conducted by the

local elected officials tasked with representing their communities. Octa therefore proposes the

following distinction on the extent of community impact information required for data center

projects under 75 MW:


       1. Sites Inside Municipal Boundaries – Projects inside municipal boundaries already

           pass through the full local regulatory framework: municipal platting and development

           ordinances, noise and nuisance regulations, lighting and setback requirements, traffic

           and driveway permitting, drainage and floodplain review, fire code and emergency

           response coordination, and water and wastewater service that the city itself allocates

           through capacity reservations and utility commitments. Therefore, these projects

           should only be required to (1) certify their locations and (2) provide all municipal

           permits and plat approvals received, in lieu of a separate ERCOT assessment.


       2. Sites Outside Municipal Boundaries – For these projects, a more comprehensive

           community impact review is warranted. Texas counties have very limited land-use and

           ordinance authority; where a facility self-supplies water or uses private utilities, no

           local body monitors usage or neighbor impacts. A state-level community impact review

           genuinely fills a gap, and Octa supports ERCOT’s proposal in that setting.


                                       III.    CONCLUSION


       Octa appreciates the Commission’s and ERCOT’s prompt response to Governor Abbott’s

August 3, 2026 directive and supports the goal of maintaining a reliable electric grid and protecting

                                                 4
 local communities. To facilitate this process, Octa respectfully requests that the Commission and

ERCOT: (a) clarify that data center projects greater than 25 MW and less than 75 MW will be

required to provide only the community impact information identified in Governor Abbott’s

August 3, 2026 letter, and not the additional verification and audit information for large loads of

75 MW or more; and (b) adopt a distinction in the scope of community impact information required

for projects inside municipal boundaries versus projects in unincorporated areas.


        ERCOT has stated that it will provide additional detail on the scope and timing of the

verification and audit process at the August 20, 2026 Open Meeting. Octa respectfully requests

that this clarification be included in that filing or process design.




Dated: August 13, 2026                          Respectfully Submitted,


                                                Anzer Husain

                                                Vice President

                                                Octa Data Center Development Company LLC

                                                a@octadatacenter.com

                     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF
     OCTA DATA CENTER DEVELOPMENT COMPANY LLC’S COMMENTS


    Scope of inquiry for projects between 25 MW and 75 MW: Octa requests that the
     Commission and ERCOT clarify that data center projects greater than 25 MW and less than
     75 MW will be required to provide only the community impact information identified in
     Governor Abbott’s August 3, 2026 letter—noise mitigation, light controls, setbacks, traffic
     improvements, emergency response coordination, and other community protection
     measures—and not the additional verification and audit information required of large loads
     of 75 MW or more.

    Distinction based on municipal boundaries: Projects under 75 MW inside municipal
     boundaries should only be required to certify their locations and provide the municipal
     permits and plat approvals they have received. For projects under 75 MW in
     unincorporated areas, where county land-use authority is limited and no local body
     monitors water use or neighbor impacts, a more comprehensive community impact review
     fills a genuine gap, and Octa supports ERCOT’s proposal in that setting.
